title: Gargi's second arrow
hookLine: the woman who was silenced stands up again, like a warrior stringing a bow, with two questions
last: THE INNER RULER LIVES IN EVERY BEING.

cards: Gargi stands up again. Two days ago she was told: don't ask too much, or your head will fall off, and she sat down. This time she speaks to the whole room first.
Honored scholars, I'll ask him two questions. If he answers them, none of you will ever beat him. Then she turns to Yajnavalkya.
As a warrior's son from Kashi or Videha strings his unstrung bow, takes two sharp arrows in his hand and rises to fight, so I rise against you with two questions. Answer them.

teach.h: SECOND ARROW: ON WHAT IS SPACE WOVEN?
teach.b: What is above the sky and below the earth and between the two, what people call past, present and future: on what is that woven? On space, Gargi. She bows.
Honor to you, Yajnavalkya, for that answer. Get ready for the second. Second arrow.
And on what is space woven? This time he doesn't stop her. He answers.

That, Gargi, is what the knowers of Brahman call the imperishable, the akshara. It is neither coarse nor fine, neither short nor long. Without shadow, without taste or smell, without eye or ear, without inside or outside.

It eats nothing, and nothing eats it. And yet at its command the sun and moon are held apart, earth and sky are held apart, and rivers run from the snowy mountains. Here's the teaching, and it's one of Hinduism's biggest.
Brahman, the one reality, isn't one more thing in the world, not even the biggest thing.

teach.h: THE IMPERISHABLE: ONLY WHAT IT ISN'T.
teach.b: It's what everything is woven on, so the Upanishad describes it almost entirely by what it isn't. That's how many Hindus can bow to a murti of Krishna or Durga at home and still say God has no edges.

teach.h: THE FORM IS WHERE YOU MEET GOD.
teach.b: As many teachers put it, the form is where you meet God, not a fence around God. And Gargi turns to the room. Count yourselves lucky if you get away by bowing to him.
None of you will beat him. Then she falls silent, on her own terms.
Tradition remembers her as a brahmavadini, a woman who spoke of Brahman, and she drew out the hardest answer of the day.

how: The akshara passage is studied in Vedanta as one of the Upanishads' great descriptions of Brahman by negation; Gargi's two questions are often retold in Hindu teaching as the moment the debate turns.

o: Gargi warned a second time, and sitting down
Gargi rising again, with two questions like arrows
Gargi coming back to claim the thousand cows

games.q: what's inside the exchange — tap the pairs.

s: Brahman and Brahma, the four-headed creator god, are the same thing
Brahma is a god with stories and a face; Brahman is the one reality, described here by what it isn't.
Gargi compares her questions to a warrior's arrows
like a warrior's son from Kashi or Videha stringing his bow.
the imperishable is described mostly by what it isn't
neither coarse nor fine, without inside or outside.

games.q: your little cousin points at the Krishna murti in the family shrine. "is that ALL of God?" using Gargi's answer, what do you say?
o: yes, all of God lives inside that statue.
we meet God there, but Brahman is what everything is woven on. no edges.
no, it's just a doll; God isn't in it at all.
games.why: the imperishable has no inside or outside. many Hindus meet God in a murti without believing God stops at its edges.

practice: Sit, and let each thing you notice be named and set down: a sound, not that; a sensation in the knee, not that; a thought, not that. Not coarse, like the chair; not fine, like the thought.
Keep setting things down, gently, without looking for what's left, and rest in the room the setting-down makes.

wordCard.voice: Akshara. The imperishable, what doesn't wear away. The same word means a syllable or a letter, and in Gargi's question, it's what even space is woven on.

orig.note: Sanskrit akṣara: a (not) + kṣara (perishing): the imperishable; also a syllable or letter.

carryVoice: Your line: brahman isn't one more thing. Next, someone asks how many gods there are. Day three hundred seventy-nine, done.
